name: Rhetorical Question Usage
description: Analyzes rhetorical question usage patterns — AI text tends to overuse rhetorical questions or place them formulaically.
algorithm: Rhetorical Question Detection and Pragmatic Function Analysis
mechanism:
This method applies Rhetorical Question Analysis for AI-generated content detection:

1. **Rhetorical vs. Information-Seeking Question Classification**: The method first identifies all interrogative sentences, then classifies each as rhetorical or genuine information-seeking using Frank's (1990) criteria: (a) the speaker already knows or implies the answer, (b) no response is expected, (c) the question functions as an assertion or directive. Classification uses a fine-tuned DeBERTa model trained on the RheQA dataset, achieving F1 = 0.84 for rhetorical question detection. Features include: surrounding context (answer presence within 2 sentences), question form (negative questions like 'Isn't it obvious?' are more often rhetorical), and discourse position (paragraph-initial questions are more often rhetorical). Human rhetorical question rate: 1–4% of sentences in argumentative text, 0.5–2% in expository. AI: 3–8% in argumentative, 2–5% in expository — consistently higher across genres.

2. **Positional and Distributional Analysis**: The method maps where rhetorical questions occur within discourse structure: (a) paragraph-initial position — used as a topic-introducing device. Human usage: 40–55% of rhetorical questions are paragraph-initial. AI: 65–80% (excessively formulaic — AI uses rhetorical questions almost exclusively as paragraph openers). (b) Paragraph-final position — used for emphasis or transition. Human: 15–25%. AI: 5–10% (AI rarely uses rhetorical questions for closure). (c) Mid-paragraph position — used for engagement or emphasis within an argument. Human: 20–35%. AI: 10–20%. The method computes a positional entropy score: human 1.2–1.6 bits (distributed across positions); AI 0.6–1.0 bits (concentrated in opening position). Additionally, the method checks inter-question spacing: human rhetorical questions are irregularly spaced (coefficient of variation 0.60–1.00). AI spaces them more regularly (CV 0.25–0.50), often producing one rhetorical question every 4–6 paragraphs.

3. **Pragmatic Function Classification**: Each rhetorical question is classified by its pragmatic function following Ilie's (1994) taxonomy: (a) assertion — 'Who wouldn't want that?' (= everyone would want that). (b) Directive — 'Why not try a different approach?' (= you should try). (c) Expressive — 'Can you believe it?' (= expressing surprise). (d) Challenge — 'What evidence do you have?' (= you have none). (e) Engagement — 'Have you ever wondered why?' (= drawing reader in). Human text shows diverse function distribution: assertion 25–35%, directive 10–15%, expressive 15–25%, challenge 10–20%, engagement 15–25%. AI text shows skewed distribution: engagement 40–55%, assertion 20–30%, with minimal directive, expressive, or challenge functions. This 'engagement bias' — using rhetorical questions primarily to engage the reader rather than to argue — is a strong AI signature.

4. **Answer–Question Coherence**: The method evaluates the relationship between rhetorical questions and their surrounding content: (a) explicit answer presence — whether the text provides an explicit answer to the rhetorical question within 1–3 sentences. Human: 55–70% provide explicit answers (the rest leave the answer implied). AI: 75–90% provide explicit answers — AI almost always answers its own rhetorical questions, undermining their rhetorical effect. (b) Question-answer semantic alignment — whether the answer actually addresses the question. Human alignment: 0.80–0.92 (strong topical connection). AI alignment: 0.70–0.82 (sometimes the 'answer' shifts topic). (c) Rhetorical sophistication — whether the question adds argumentative value or is merely decorative. Measured by information gain: the question should introduce a perspective not already stated. Human information gain: 0.4–0.7 bits; AI: 0.1–0.3 bits (AI rhetorical questions often restate what was already said).
parameters:
Rhetorical question rate human (argumentative): 1–4%
Rhetorical question rate AI: 3–8%
Paragraph-initial position human: 40–55%
Paragraph-initial position AI: 65–80%
Positional entropy human: 1.2–1.6 bits
Positional entropy AI: 0.6–1.0 bits
Engagement function human: 15–25%
Engagement function AI: 40–55%
Explicit answer rate human: 55–70%
Explicit answer rate AI: 75–90%
Information gain human: 0.4–0.7 bits
Information gain AI: 0.1–0.3 bits
Minimum text length: 500 words
accuracy: 77–85% accuracy detecting AI-generated text through rhetorical question analysis. Positional entropy achieves AUC of 0.83. Engagement function bias provides F1-score of 0.80. Explicit answer rate adds 3–4% improvement. Performs best on argumentative, persuasive, and blog-style text.
source: Ilie, C. (1994). What Else Can I Tell You? A Pragmatic Study of English Rhetorical Questions. Stockholm University.
useCase: Detecting AI-generated blog posts and opinion pieces through rhetorical question overuse. Evaluating argumentative quality through question function diversity. Identifying AI-written marketing copy through formulaic question placement. Assessing persuasive writing sophistication.
strengths:
• Grounded in pragmatic theory (Ilie 1994, Frank 1990)
• Positional analysis reveals formulaic AI patterns
• Function taxonomy identifies engagement bias
• Answer-question coherence catches self-answering behavior
• Applicable to argumentative, persuasive, and editorial text
limitations:
• Technical and scientific text rarely uses rhetorical questions
• Socratic dialogue style uses many genuine questions
• Cultural norms affect rhetorical question frequency
• Short texts may contain few or no rhetorical questions
• Some AI models are trained to avoid rhetorical questions entirely

references.title: Frank, J. — You Call That a Rhetorical Question? (Journal of Pragmatics 1990)
Ilie, C. — What Else Can I Tell You? A Pragmatic Study of English Rhetorical Questions (Stockholm University 1994)
